passages.t: Free from the law, joined to Christ
passages.happening:
Paul speaks to those “who know the law” (verse 1). The law has authority over a person only as long as he lives.

He gives an example from marriage. A married woman is bound by law to her husband as long as he lives. If he dies, she is released (verse 2). If she joins another man while her husband is alive, she is called an adulteress; but if he dies, she is free to marry again (verse 3).

“Therefore, my brothers, you also died to the law through the body of Christ, that you might belong to another, to Him who was raised from the dead, in order that we might bear fruit to God” (verse 4).

When we lived ‘according to the flesh’, sinful passions stirred up by the law were at work in us, bearing fruit for death (verse 5). “But now, having died to what bound us, we have been released from the law, so that we serve in the new way of the Spirit, and not in the old way of the written code” (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
‘Those who know the law’ could mean Jewish believers who knew the law of Moses, or anyone who knew how law works in general. Roman law and Jewish law agreed on the point Paul makes: a law binds the living, not the dead.

The marriage picture is not exact at every step, and Paul does not need it to be. In the picture the husband dies; in Paul's meaning, it is the believer who has ‘died to the law’ by sharing Christ's death. The main point is simple: death ends an old bond and leaves a person free to belong to another.

‘Belong to another’ continues the marriage picture. Believers now belong to the risen Christ, and the fruit of that union is a life given to God.

‘According to the flesh’ means human life turned away from God, weak and bent toward sin. Paul says something startling in verse 5: the law, instead of calming sinful desires, actually stirred them up. He explains how in the verses that follow.

‘The new way of the Spirit’ and ‘the old way of the written code’ pick up 2:29. The law written on stone told people what to do. The Spirit writes God's will on the heart and gives the power to do it. Paul will fill this out in chapter 8.
passages.ot:
The law of Moses spoke of a wife released from a first marriage who “becomes another man's wife” (Deuteronomy 24:2). Paul's picture would be familiar.

The prophets often pictured God's bond with his people as a marriage. Through Hosea, God says, “So I will betroth you to Me forever; I will betroth you in righteousness and justice, in loving devotion and compassion” (Hosea 2:19). Paul pictures believers joined to the risen Christ.

The ‘new way of the Spirit’ echoes the new covenant of Jeremiah 31:33, the law written on the heart, and Ezekiel's promise: “I will put My Spirit within you and cause you to walk in My statutes” (Ezekiel 36:27).
passages.hard: Does ‘released from the law’ mean that God's commands no longer matter for Christians? Christians answer carefully here. Paul does not say the law is bad; a few verses later he calls it holy and good (verse 12). He says believers are released from the law as a power that binds and condemns, and from the law as the old covenant's way of ordering life. Churches differ on how much of the law of Moses still guides believers. Many distinguish its moral commands, which they see as still showing God's will, from its rules for worship and for Israel's life as a nation. Others put the stress on Christ's own teaching and the Spirit's leading. All agree that the freedom Paul means is freedom to ‘bear fruit to God’, not freedom to sin.
passages.asks: Paul says believers belong to another: the risen Christ. Ask what has had a hold on you, a rule, a voice, a fear of failing, that you serve out of duty and dread. Then ask what it would mean to serve ‘in the new way of the Spirit’, out of love for the one you belong to.

passages.t: Is the law sin? The commandment and the deceiver
passages.happening:
“What then shall we say? Is the law sin? Certainly not!” (verse 7). I would not have known sin except through the law. I would not have known what coveting was if the law had not said, ‘Do not covet’ (verse 7).

“But sin, seizing its opportunity through the commandment, produced in me every kind of covetous desire. For apart from the law, sin is dead” (verse 8).

“Once I was alive apart from the law; but when the commandment came, sin sprang to life and I died” (verse 9). The very commandment that was meant to bring life brought death (verse 10). For sin, seizing its chance through the commandment, deceived me and killed me (verse 11).

“So then, the law is holy, and the commandment is holy, righteous, and good” (verse 12). Did what is good bring death to me? Certainly not. It was sin, using what was good, so that sin would be shown up for what it is, utterly sinful (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
Paul now switches to ‘I’. Who the ‘I’ is will be the great question of the next passage. Here many readers hear echoes of Adam in Eden, or of Israel receiving the law at Sinai, or of Paul's own life as a boy who came to know the commandments. The note on 7:14-25 sets out the views.

Notice which commandment Paul picks: ‘Do not covet’. It is the tenth commandment, and the only one that is entirely about the heart. A person can keep from stealing and still want what is not his. Coveting shows that sin lives inside, not only in what we do.

Sin is pictured almost as a person: it ‘seizes its opportunity’, it ‘springs to life’, it ‘deceives’. The commandment is like a fence that tells you where you must not go, and sin uses it to make you want to climb over.

So the law is not the villain. Paul is firm: it is ‘holy, righteous, and good’. The villain is sin, which takes something good and turns it into a trap. The law did one thing well: it showed sin up as sin.
passages.ot:
The commandment Paul quotes is the tenth: “You shall not covet your neighbor's house. You shall not covet your neighbor's wife” (Exodus 20:17).

The commandment ‘meant to bring life’ echoes the promise of the law: “Keep My statutes and My judgments, for the man who does these things will live by them” (Leviticus 18:5).

Sin that ‘deceived me’ echoes Eve's words in the garden: “The serpent deceived me,” she replied, “and I ate.” (Genesis 3:13). There, too, a good command became the place where a deceiver struck, and death followed.
passages.hard: Does the law make people sin more? Paul says that sin used the commandment to stir up desire. Many people know this: being told not to do something can make us want it more. But Paul does not blame the law. He blames sin, which twists the good. His point is that the problem is not a lack of good rules. It is the human heart. That is why the answer cannot be more rules, but rescue, which he will name in verse 25 and describe in chapter 8.
passages.asks: Paul chose the commandment about wanting. Ask what you covet: someone's life, looks, family, money, success. Notice how a ‘no’ can make you want it more. Then ask whether you have treated God's commands as the enemy, when the real enemy is the sin that twists them.

passages.t: ‘I do not do what I want’
passages.happening:
“We know that the law is spiritual; but I am unspiritual, sold as a slave to sin” (verse 14).

“I do not understand what I do. For what I want to do, I do not do. But what I hate, I do” (verse 15). If I do what I do not want, I agree that the law is good (verse 16). So it is no longer I who do it, but sin living in me (verse 17).

“I know that nothing good lives in me, that is, in my flesh; for I have the desire to do what is good, but I cannot carry it out” (verse 18). “For I do not do the good I want to do. Instead, I keep on doing the evil I do not want to do” (verse 19). If so, it is sin living in me that does it (verse 20).

So I find this rule at work: when I want to do good, evil is right there with me (verse 21). “For in my inner being I delight in God’s law” (verse 22). But another law is at work in my body, at war with the law of my mind and holding me captive to sin (verse 23).

“What a wretched man I am! Who will rescue me from this body of death?” (verse 24). “Thanks be to God, through Jesus Christ our Lord!” (verse 25). So with my mind I serve the law of God, but with my flesh the law of sin (verse 25).
passages.hearers:
This is one of the most honest passages ever written about the human heart. Paul's hearers would recognise the struggle, and so do readers today. Greek and Roman writers knew it too. The Roman poet Ovid, writing a little before Paul, has Medea say that she sees the better way and approves it, yet follows the worse (Metamorphoses, book 7). The struggle between knowing the good and doing it was an old theme.

Paul uses the present tense here: ‘I do’, ‘I want’, ‘I hate’. In verses 7 to 13 he used the past. That change is one reason readers argue about who the ‘I’ is.

‘Sold as a slave to sin’ uses the picture of the slave market again. A slave sold to a master cannot do as he chooses.

‘Nothing good lives in me, that is, in my flesh’. Paul is careful. He does not say he is nothing but bad. There is an ‘inner being’ that delights in God's law. The problem is that wanting is not enough.

Then the cry: “What a wretched man I am!” (verse 24). It is not the end of the passage. The answer comes at once, as thanks: rescue is through Jesus Christ. Chapter 8 will show how.
passages.ot:
The ‘inner being’ that delights in God's law sounds like the Psalms: “his delight is in the Law of the LORD, and on His law he meditates day and night” (Psalm 1:2), and “Oh, how I love Your law!” (Psalm 119:97).

The prophets knew the heart's trouble too. Jeremiah says, “The heart is deceitful above all things and beyond cure. Who can understand it?” (Jeremiah 17:9), close to Paul's ‘I do not understand what I do’. And David prays for what only God can give: “Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me” (Psalm 51:10).
passages.hard:
Who is the ‘I’ in verses 14 to 25? This is a real question on which faithful Christians differ, and these notes do not choose.

One reading says Paul describes the present struggle of a believer. Augustine came to hold this in his later writings, after first reading it otherwise, and Luther, Calvin and much of the Lutheran and Reformed tradition have followed. They point to the present tense, to the person who ‘delights in God's law’ (verse 22), and to verse 25, which states the struggle again after the thanks.

A second reading says Paul describes a person under the law without the Spirit, looking back from faith. Many early church writers, and many modern scholars, hold this. They point out that this ‘I’ is ‘sold as a slave to sin’, while chapter 6 says believers have been set free, and that the Spirit, named so often in chapter 8, is not named here.

A third reading hears Paul speaking ‘in character’, a known way of writing, for Adam in Eden (verses 9 to 11 echo Genesis 3), or for Israel under the law, or for anyone trying to live by the law in their own strength. The early writer Origen read the passage in this way.

Many combine these. On every reading, the law is good, sin is the problem, and rescue comes through Jesus Christ.

If you are worn down by failing again and again, or caught in an addiction you cannot break, you are not alone, and you are not beyond help. Paul's cry was answered with thanks. Please talk to someone: a doctor, a pastor, a counsellor, or a group that helps people with what you are facing. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Paul is honest about his struggle. Ask where you know this fight: the good you want and do not do, the thing you hate and do again. Then notice where Paul looks. Not inward for more willpower, but outward: ‘Who will rescue me?’ Ask whether you have stopped asking that question, and who you could ask for help.
